6.name: Responsible Use, Data Protection, and Governance

docs.t: Building a Prompt That Fits the Job
docs.x: Prompt Construction. A first response is only as good as the specification behind it. Give Claude the role, the context it cannot know, one clear task, the constraints and the output format, scaled to what the job needs.

docs.t: Building a Prompt That Fits the Job
docs.x: Most weak first responses are not model failures. They are specification failures: the request left out something only the person asking knew. The AI Fluency framework calls the skill of specifying work Description .

docs.t: Building a Prompt That Fits the Job
docs.x: Component What it controls Typical gap Role Vocabulary, depth and point of view Rarely the main problem on its own Context Audience, situation, prior decisions, source material The most often missing component Task The one action wanted: summarize, compare, draft, identify A vague verb such as "review" or "look at" Constraints Length, tone, what to include or avoid, house rules Output the wrong length or tone, or invented terms Output format Table, bullets, memo, email, fixed headings Outputs that cannot be compared or reused Not every request needs all five. A quick question needs a task. A client deliverable needs all five.

docs.t: Building a Prompt That Fits the Job
docs.h: Context Claude does not have by default
docs.x: Claude cannot see your inbox, org chart, last meeting, pricing rules or the decision a document will support, unless you supply it or connect a source. When context is missing, Claude fills the gap with something plausible: a generic paragraph, a typical policy, an invented incentive. "Summarize our Q3 results" returns three paragraphs that could describe any company. "Summarize the attached Q3 data for our regional director, who cares about cost and throughput. Cover only metrics that moved more than 10% against target, as a headline and three one-sentence bullets" returns a draft that needs two minutes of editing.

docs.t: Building a Prompt That Fits the Job
docs.h: Grounding and permission to say "not covered"
docs.x: For factual work, add two lines: answer only from the material provided, and say when it does not cover something. This turns open-ended writing into bounded use of your sources, and it is the cheapest defense against invented facts.

docs.t: Building a Prompt That Fits the Job
docs.c: Roles and adjectives do not add facts
docs.x: When a style is hard to describe ("casual and question-led"), one or two short examples show it more precisely than adjectives do. "You are a world-class expert" and "make it more persuasive" feel like improvements, but they give Claude no facts. If the draft is generic or wrong, look for the missing context first.

docs.h: Apply it: Specify Brightwater's campaign brief
docs.x: An account executive types: "Write social posts for the spring sale." The client is the smaller of the two grocery chains. The posts must use the client's name exactly as "FreshWay Market," never mention competitors, stay under 200 characters and drive sign-ups for the loyalty app. 1. List what Claude cannot know from the one-line request. 2. Rewrite the request with all five components. 3. Add one line that prevents invented facts. Done when: the first response would need only light editing. 1. Missing context. Who the client is, the sale dates and offer, the audience (loyalty-app prospects), the goal (sign-ups), the brand rules (exact name, no competitors) and the length limit. 2. Rewritten request. "You write social copy for FreshWay Market, a regional grocery chain. Audience: shoppers in San Diego County who do not yet use the FreshWay app. Task: draft five posts for the spring sale (20% off produce, 4 to 18 April) that drive downloads of the loyalty app. Constraints: write the name exactly as 'FreshWay Market'; never mention or compare with other grocers; under 200 characters each; friendly, not pushy. Format: a numbered list, each post followed by a suggested hashtag." 3. Grounding line. "Use only the offer details above; if something you need is missing, say so instead of inventing it." - Every gap in step 1 is closed in the rewrite. - Brand rules are stated as constraints, not left to Claude. - The output format is explicit. - The request forbids invented offers or facts.

Task Decomposition and Sequencing. Deliverables with several distinct parts are several tasks. Run them as ordered steps, check each intermediate result before the next step builds on it, and match the prompting strategy to each step's task type.

A request such as "evaluate these four bids and choose a winner" hides four tasks: agree criteria, score each bid, weigh trade-offs, recommend. Asked in one prompt, Claude does each shallowly and the reasoning is invisible. Decomposition turns it into ordered steps, each producing a result you can check.

docs.h: Order the steps from foundation to synthesis
docs.c: Put a checkpoint where an error would spread
docs.x: 1. Requirements or criteria first, so every later step has a target. 2. Extraction and computation next. Numbers come from code execution, not prose. 3. Analysis or comparison on the checked inputs. 4. Synthesis last: the recommendation, summary or message built from finished parts. Check the step that every later step depends on: the extracted list, the computed figures, the criteria. A wrong number caught there costs a minute; caught in the board pack it costs a meeting.

When one source feeds several outputs (an all-staff email, a manager pack and an FAQ from one strategy), extract and confirm the shared content once, then draft each output from that confirmed list. Drafting each from the raw source invites three slightly different stories.

Task type Tighten Loosen Analysis Criteria, standards, scope Phrasing Research Question, sources, citations How findings are synthesized Drafting Audience, tone, format Word choice Brainstorming Goal and a few guardrails Volume and range A staged campaign workflow uses loose prompts to generate concepts, then tight criteria to score them, then a detailed brief for the winner. Mixing the two in one prompt kills the range of ideas.

Keep dependent steps in one conversation so each step sees the previous one. Run independent steps in separate conversations. When a conversation grows long, carry forward a checked summary rather than the whole thread. Work that spans days and reuses the same sources belongs in a Project . Asking for the recommendation first and the evidence afterwards produces reasoning that justifies the answer instead of testing it.

Items describe a single prompt that produced shallow or untraceable work, or a multi-step workflow where an error slipped through. Choose the sequence that builds a checked foundation first and the checkpoint that sits right after the step everything else depends on. Distractors ask for a longer single response, reverse the order, or check only at the end.

docs.h: Apply it: Decompose Ironwood's carrier review
docs.x: Procurement must recommend which of five carriers to keep for next year. Inputs: last year's shipment records (a spreadsheet), each carrier's contract and scorecard, and a budget limit. Last quarter a miscalculated on-time rate nearly dropped a good carrier. 1. Break the work into ordered steps. 2. Mark each step as Claude, Claude with code execution, or a person. 3. Place the checkpoints and say what each checks. Done when: a wrong on-time rate could not reach the recommendation. 1 and 2. Steps. 1. Agree evaluation criteria and weights (on-time rate, damage claims, cost, contract terms) with the procurement manager. Person, drafted with Claude. 2. Compute on-time rate and damage-claim rate per carrier from the shipment records. Claude with code execution. 3. Extract key contract terms (price per mile, penalties, notice periods) into one table. Claude. 4. Score each carrier against the weighted criteria. Claude, from the checked inputs. 5. Draft the recommendation with trade-offs. Claude. 6. Decide and approve. Procurement manager. 3. Checkpoints. After step 1: criteria and weights approved. After step 2: spot-check two carriers' rates against the raw records and confirm the calculation logic. After step 3: compare the table with each contract's notice and penalty clauses. Before step 6: the manager reviews the scoring table, not just the conclusion. - Criteria come first and are approved by a person. - Rates are computed with code execution and spot-checked. - Contract extraction is checked against the contracts. - The decision stays with the procurement manager.

Prompt Diagnosis and Iteration. Read a disappointing output as evidence. Name the specification gap it points to (missing context, ambiguous instruction, absent constraint or wrong strategy), change that one thing, and know when to stop iterating, restart or change approach.

When output disappoints, two habits waste time: giving up ("Claude can't do this") and thrashing (changing many things at once). Diagnosis replaces both: read the output, name the gap, fix that component.

Symptom Likely gap Fix Generic, could be about anyone Missing context Add audience, facts, purpose A reasonable answer to a different question Ambiguous instruction Sharpen the verb and scope ("check whether each conclusion follows from the tables") Right content, wrong length, tone or shape Absent constraint Add the limit, tone or format Good explanation, wrong numbers Wrong strategy : prose arithmetic Use code execution Confident but out of date Wrong strategy : no current source Web search or Research Narrow, safe brainstorm Wrong strategy : over-constrained Loosen, then filter later Correct early, drifting later in a long chat Context degradation Restart with a summary

docs.h: Change one thing at a time
docs.x: Keep the parts that work and change the component the output points to. If you rewrite the whole prompt, you lose what worked and cannot tell which change helped. Round 1 added the cause and the new date to a delay notice. Round 2 added a tone limit. Round 3 asked only for a better subject line. Round 4 would have changed a single word, so the writer finished by hand.

docs.h: When to stop, restart or change approach
docs.x: - Stop iterating when rounds produce marginal change; finish with a manual edit. - Restart with a summary when a long conversation has degraded. - Change approach when the same failure survives several rounds. Nine rounds of fixing one format element and breaking another show that a fixed multi-step format belongs in a Skill or template, not in more prompting. - Reshape the task when it asks for something no prompt can deliver, such as an exact future sales figure. Ask for scenarios and ranges instead. Switching to the most capable model is the expensive move and rarely the fix for a specification gap. A stronger model cannot supply facts the request never contained.

Items show a prompt, its output and the author's real goal. Name the gap from the evidence: first response wrong (specification), numbers wrong (strategy), outdated facts (strategy), drifting late (context), repeated failure on a fixed format (approach). Distractors switch models, regenerate, rewrite everything or add adjectives.

docs.h: Apply it: Diagnose Fairhaven's quiz prompt
docs.x: Ms. Rivera asked: "Make a quiz on chapter 4 of our novel." She got 25 recall questions about minor characters, too hard for her Grade 8 class, with no answer key. She wanted 10 questions on theme and character motivation for a 20-minute warm-up, with answers. 1. Name each gap and the component it belongs to. 2. Write the improved request. 3. Say what you would do if round two still misses on one element. Done when: each fix targets a named gap. 1. Gaps. - Purpose and focus (theme and motivation, not recall): missing context and a vague task . - Grade level: missing context . - Count and time (10 questions, 20 minutes): absent constraints . - Answer key: missing output format . 2. Improved request. "For a Grade 8 English class that has just read chapter 4 of the novel (attached), write 10 questions for a 20-minute warm-up. Focus on theme and characters' motivations, not plot recall. Mix 6 short-answer and 4 multiple-choice questions at a Grade 8 reading level. Format: numbered questions, then an answer key with one-sentence explanations." 3. If one element still misses (for example, the multiple-choice questions are too easy), keep the rest of the request and change only that instruction, for example "make the multiple-choice distractors plausible misreadings of the chapter." Stop when changes become marginal and finish by hand. - Each gap is tied to one component. - The improved request closes every gap. - The next iteration changes one thing, not everything.

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Output Evaluation and Fitness for Purpose. Judge every output against three references (the requirements, the sources and the professional standard) and check completeness separately from accuracy. Then classify it as ready to use, needs revision or needs human correction.

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Output that reads well is not the same as output that is fit for purpose. The AI Fluency framework calls the skill of judging output Discernment . It is a check against fixed references, run the same way every time, not a feeling about whether a draft looks good.

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Reference The question Example failure Requirements Does it do everything that was asked, and nothing that was not? A proofread that also rewrote two contract clauses Sources Do claims match the documents supplied? "$12 per unit" without "minimum 5,000 units" Professional standards Would it pass in this field and for this audience? An accurate letter that ignores a bilingual requirement

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Accuracy asks whether what is there is right. Completeness asks whether anything that matters is missing. A security summary can be correct on every point and still omit breach notification, the reader's main concern. Missing things are harder to see than wrong ones, so check against what the reader needs, deliberately. Claude flagged four invoice mismatches, and all four were real. That proves nothing about the 56 invoices it passed. Sampling the unflagged ones is the only way to find misses.

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Verdict When Next step Ready to use Meets requirements, matches sources, clears the standard for its use Normal review, then use Needs revision Close, with a specific gap Name the gap, re-prompt or edit, re-check Needs human correction Stakes, errors or uncertainty mean the draft cannot stand A qualified person takes over; the draft can still guide them Calibrate to the use. An internal brainstorm with a few generic ideas is ready as a discussion starter. A regulatory gap analysis done without the regulation text needs a specialist, however confident it sounds. Polished formatting, confident tone and correct spelling say nothing about fitness. Equally, a blanket rule such as "AI drafts always need three rounds" ignores the evaluation.

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Items give an output, its purpose and the sources, and ask for the verdict or the missing check. Look for the specific gap: an omitted condition, a missing reader concern, a change beyond the request, an audience mismatch. Distractors accept the draft because the numbers match, discard it entirely, or check only formatting.

docs.t: Is This Output Fit for Purpose?
docs.x: Member services has three Claude drafts: (A) a reply explaining the overdraft fee policy to a member, accurate but stiff, for a member who mentioned a death in the family; (B) a board summary of a new regulation, written without the regulation attached; (C) an internal list of ideas for reducing branch wait times. 1. Run the three references for each draft. 2. Give each a verdict and the reason. 3. State the next step for each. Done when: every verdict names a specific reference. A. Needs revision. Requirements and sources pass (the fee policy is correct), but the professional standard for a grieving member fails on tone. Next step: the agent rewrites the reply with empathy and checks the policy details against the member's account before sending. B. Needs human correction. The source check cannot be done because the regulation was never supplied, and the stakes are regulatory. Next step: the compliance team uses the draft as a starting list, checks every point against the regulation text and owns the board summary. C. Ready to use as an internal discussion starter. No sources to check, low stakes, easily revised. Next step: share with the branch managers' meeting. - Each verdict cites requirements, sources or standards. - B is not accepted on confidence alone. - C is not over-reviewed.

Hallucination Detection and Verification. Fluent output can contain invented citations, confident specifics, contradictions, bias and claims of actions Claude never took. Learn the signatures, prevent them in the prompt, and verify against an independent source before anything is used.

Claude writes with the same assurance whether it is right or wrong. A fabricated statistic reads exactly like a verified one. You catch hallucinations by knowing their signatures and checking against sources, not by waiting for something to look wrong.

docs.c: Precision is a warning sign, not evidence
docs.x: Pattern What it looks like Confident invented specifics "31.4% market share" with no source, from a chat without search Fabricated citations An author, journal and volume that no database can find Unsupported claims in a summary A figure that does not appear in the uploaded report Internal contradictions 400 customers on page 2, 650 on page 9 Outdated knowledge Detailed "obligations" of a law passed after the training cutoff Bias from framing "Which features do customers like, especially the new dashboard?" returns praise for the dashboard Claimed actions "I've emailed the team" or "I saved it to your Drive" with no connected tool The more specific an unsourced claim, the more authoritative it looks. Specific numbers, names, quotes and dates are exactly what must be traced to a source.

- Restrict answers to the provided sources and permit "I don't know" or "not covered." - Ask for the exact supporting quote or section for each claim. - For current facts, use web search or Research , which return citations you can open.

1. Trace each key claim to its source: open the cited page or find the passage. 2. Check currency : a real citation can still be last year's figure. 3. Recompute derived numbers (margins, totals) with code execution. 4. Read long outputs whole for consistency. 5. Confirm claimed actions in the actual system. "Are you sure?" and "add a note that this is verified" are not verification. Neither is regenerating and comparing. Independent confirmation means a source outside the output. Grounded citations from Research are checkable, which is their value, but they still need checking: a source can be paraphrased wrongly or taken out of context.

Items present an output with a suspicious specific, a citation that cannot be found, a contradiction or a claimed action. Pick the step that checks against an independent source, or the prompt change that grounds the answer. Distractors trust confidence, round the number, add a label, average two figures or ask Claude to vouch for itself.

docs.h: Apply it: Verify Brightwater's press release
docs.x: A Claude draft press release for a client's new store says: the store is "the largest organic grocery in Southern California"; it "created 120 local jobs"; a quote from the client's CEO; and "shoppers save an average of 18% versus competitors." The release goes to media tomorrow. 1. List each claim and its risk pattern. 2. Say how to verify each and who confirms it. 3. Decide what happens to claims that cannot be confirmed. Done when: nothing unsourced remains in the release. 1 and 2. Claims. - "Largest organic grocery in Southern California": a superlative with no source. Verify against a published industry ranking or remove; the client must be able to substantiate it. - "120 local jobs": a specific figure. Confirm with the client's HR or press office. - CEO quote: attributed to a real person. The CEO approves the exact wording in writing. - "Average 18% savings versus competitors": a comparative claim about rivals, with legal risk. Requires the client's documented price study; otherwise remove. 3. Unconfirmed claims are removed or rewritten as statements the client can support ("one of the region's largest organic selections" only if substantiated). Priya Nair approves the final release, and the client approves the quote. - Every specific, superlative and quote is traced to a source or approval. - Comparative claims about competitors need documentation. - Unconfirmed claims are removed, not softened by rounding.

Review Depth and Escalation. Set review depth by what happens if the output is wrong. Consequence, reversibility, audience and regulatory exposure decide whether a quick read is enough, every fact needs checking, or a qualified person must review or take over.

Accountability does not transfer to the tool. Work produced with Claude is your work once you use or send it, held to the same standard as if you had produced it alone. The AI Fluency framework calls this Diligence . The question is not whether to review, but how deeply.

Factor Ask Raises the bar Consequence of error What does a mistake cost, and whom? Money, health, legal rights, a person's job Reversibility Can it be caught and undone before harm? Sent, filed, published, paid Audience Who will see it? External, executive, regulator, the public Regulatory exposure Does a rule, contract or law govern it? Filings, disclosures, regulated advice

Output Depth Internal agenda, brainstorm, personal notes A quick read for sense Internal analysis feeding a team decision Check key facts and figures Client deliverable, board figures, public post Verify every claim; recompute numbers; approval before release Medical, legal, financial advice or decisions about people Review by a qualified, accountable professional for every item From one CRM export, a weekly call list for reps needs a light check, while the board revenue slide needs every figure independently recomputed.

docs.h: Decide in advance; do not lower the bar quietly
docs.x: The do-not-send-without-review list (client deliverables, financially material figures, regulated or confidential content, public and legal statements) should be fixed before the deadline arrives. A good pilot does not lower the standard for high-consequence content, and a dollar threshold does not remove regulatory exposure.

docs.c: Passing the checking to the reader
docs.x: When rounds of prompting stop improving a high-stakes draft, the next step is a person, not another prompt. When the reviewer lacks the expertise (a new regulator, a clinical question), escalate to someone who has it. "The committee will catch errors" or "the client can check the figure" shifts responsibility to people who are not accountable for your work.

Items describe an output and its use, and ask how much review it needs, who must review it, or what is wrong with a proposal to reduce review. Weigh the four factors. Distractors apply one standard to everything, rely on a good pilot, use a value threshold for regulated work, or trust Claude's own confidence.

docs.h: Apply it: Set Fairhaven's review rules
docs.x: The HR team wants one rule for reviewing Claude-drafted answers to staff questions. About 70% are routine (pay dates, holiday schedule); others concern medical leave, disability accommodations and disputes about pay. 1. Sort the question types by the four factors. 2. Write the review rule for each group. 3. Name who reviews and when. Done when: routine answers are fast and sensitive ones are protected. 1. Groups. - Routine (pay dates, holidays, forms): low consequence, easily corrected, internal. - Benefits figures (deductibles, leave balances): moderate consequence; a wrong number affects choices. - Medical leave, accommodations, pay disputes: high consequence, legal duties, sensitive. 2 and 3. Rules. - Routine: an HR generalist reads the draft before sending; answers cite the handbook section. - Benefits figures: the generalist checks each figure against the current plan document before sending. - Sensitive: the draft goes to the HR specialist, who checks against law and policy and sends it personally; Claude may help with wording only. - Review depth differs by group, not one rule for all. - Sensitive cases go to an accountable specialist before sending. - Figures are checked against the current source.

docs.t: Adapting Output and Choosing the Format
docs.x: Output Adaptation and Format Selection. Claude drafts; you deliver. Edit for clarity, tone and the reader, choose the format by how the output will be used, and compute any number that must be exact instead of letting it be written as prose.

docs.t: Adapting Output and Choosing the Format
docs.x: An accurate draft is not yet a deliverable. The gap is the editing pass, where you apply your knowledge of the audience and the channel.

docs.t: Adapting Output and Choosing the Format
docs.x: Audience Lead with Keep Leave out Executives The decision and its impact A few key numbers Method detail Working team What to do, who owns it Detail and evidence Executive framing External or public What they need to know or do Plain language Internal detail and anything that identifies individuals The facts stay the same; selection, depth and tone change. Adapting for an external audience also decides what is disclosed : small-area counts or quotes from a confidential source can identify people.

docs.t: Adapting Output and Choosing the Format
docs.h: Choose the format by use and reliability
docs.c: Compute, do not write, numbers that matter
docs.x: Format Use it for Inline reply Quick answers acted on in the chat Artifact Substantial, self-contained content you will edit or reuse, including small interactive tools Structured data (tables, fixed columns) Data people will sort or load into another tool Code-executed result Any number that must be exact: totals, rates, margins File creation or a Skill Real Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files, especially in a fixed template A total written in prose is a plausible guess. Code execution runs the calculation on the actual data and makes it checkable. Claude still writes the code, so read the logic (for example, how "retained customer" was defined) or spot-check a few rows.

docs.t: Adapting Output and Choosing the Format
docs.x: When quality matters, generate two or three drafts and edit the strongest, instead of rescuing the first one. The final version still needs your review. Sending the same full draft to executives and the working team serves neither. A 14-finding analysis for a 10-minute meeting needs the three findings that matter most, with the full set in a reference document.

docs.t: Adapting Output and Choosing the Format
docs.x: Items give a raw output plus its audience or channel and ask for the best adaptation or format. Match the format to use (scan on a phone, load into a spreadsheet, edit over several rounds, present to a board) and use code execution for exact numbers. Distractors keep jargon, send one version to all audiences, or rely on prose arithmetic.

docs.h: Apply it: Adapt Ironwood's weekly report
docs.x: Claude produced one long weekly analysis: on-time shipments fell from 95% to 89% at two sites because of a carrier change and new hires; overtime rose 14%. The VP Operations has five minutes; the two site managers must act this week. Figures came from Claude's prose reading of the spreadsheets. 1. Fix the reliability problem first. 2. Write the VP version (three to five lines). 3. Outline the site-manager version. Done when: each version fits its reader and the numbers are computed. 1. Reliability. Recompute on-time rates and overtime with code execution on the Monday spreadsheets; check the two sites' figures against the raw rows before anything is sent. 2. VP version. "On-time shipments fell to 89% (target 95%) at Joplin and Wichita this week. Cause: the switch to a new regional carrier plus four new pickers still in training. Overtime is up 14% as a result. Ask: approve one week of the previous carrier on the Joplin route while the new one is retrained." 3. Site-manager version. Per site: computed on-time rate by day and route, the late loads with carrier and cause, the training schedule for new pickers with owner and dates, and the overtime by shift, with actions due Friday. - Numbers are recomputed before adaptation. - The VP version leads with impact and the decision needed. - The site version keeps detail and assigns actions.

Capability Selection. Pick capabilities from what the task needs. Chat for one-offs, Projects for recurring context, Artifacts and file creation for deliverables, web search or Research for current information, code execution for exact numbers, Skills for repeatable procedures, connectors for live data, and memory for continuity.
Before writing a prompt, decide where and with what you will work. The capability choice sets the ceiling on what the session can produce.

Capability Use it when Not for Chat One-off questions and drafts Work you will repeat with the same background Projects Recurring work with stable context: instructions plus a knowledge base used by every chat in it A single reply Artifacts Substantial content to edit or reuse; small interactive tools Quick answers Web search A quick current fact Deep multi-source investigation Research A cited report from many searches that build on each other (takes minutes, uses more of the plan) Single facts Code execution and file creation Exact calculations, cleaning data, producing real Excel, Word, PowerPoint or PDF files Writing prose Skills A repeatable procedure or template applied the same way every time, by anyone One-off tasks Connectors Reaching live data in tools you can already access, such as Google Drive, Gmail and Calendar Public web content Memory Recurring facts about you and your work carried across chats Firm rules, documents, procedures

A quarterly funder report might use a Project (requirements and template), code execution (outcome metrics), Research (sector context with citations) and file creation (the funder's Word template). Name the need for each step, then the capability. Does the task recur? Is the background context the same each time? Is the output format consistent? If at least two answers are yes, a Project usually repays its setup within a few sessions.

- Connectors work within your own permissions . Each connector has defined actions, may ask for approval before acting, and admins can restrict or disable them. - Built-in knowledge stops at a training cutoff ; recent events need search or Research. - Skills need code execution and file creation turned on, and they live at account level , so a Skill can be used in any Project. A one-off reply to a supplier does not need a Project or a new Skill. Overbuilding wastes the time the tool should save.

Items describe a task and ask which capability or combination fits. Read for the need: recurring context, current information, exact numbers, a real file, a fixed procedure across people, live private data, or continuity. Distractors use Research for private data, memory as a document store, incognito where context is needed, or a plain chat for recurring work.

docs.h: Apply it: Choose capabilities for Fairhaven
docs.x: The communications office wants help with three tasks: (A) a monthly parent newsletter in English and Spanish built from the district events calendar in Google Calendar, in a fixed template; (B) a one-time reply to a reporter's question about the bus schedule, with the schedule PDF at hand; (C) a cited overview of how other districts handled cell-phone policies this year. 1. Choose the capabilities for each task. 2. Justify each choice in one line. 3. Name one capability you would not use for each, and why. Done when: each choice maps to a stated need. A. A Project (template, tone rules, bilingual requirement in instructions), the Calendar connector (live events) and a Skill or file creation for the newsletter template. Not memory: rules and templates need dependable configuration. B. A plain chat with the PDF attached. One-off, source in hand. Not a Project: no recurrence. C. Research, then open and check the key citations. Current, multi-source and cited. Not built-in knowledge: policies changed this year, after the training cutoff. - Recurring work uses a Project; the one-off does not. - Live private data comes through a connector. - Current external information comes from Research with checked citations.

docs.t: Choosing a Model and Effort Level
docs.x: Model and Effort Selection. Match the model tier and effort level to the task's complexity, stakes, speed and cost. Use faster, lighter settings for structured, high-volume, low-stakes work, more capability and effort for ambiguous, consequential work, and be able to defend the choice.

docs.t: Choosing a Model and Effort Level
docs.x: Claude models come in tiers, from fast and efficient to most capable. Effort is a separate setting: how much thinking Claude applies to a response. Higher capability and higher effort tend to give more thorough answers on complex work, but take longer and use more of the plan's allowance. Model names change; the decision logic does not.

docs.t: Choosing a Model and Effort Level
docs.x: Task profile Typical choice Classification, extraction, formatting, short templated replies, high volume, easy to correct Fast tier (such as Haiku), default or low effort Most drafting, synthesis and analysis Balanced tier (such as Sonnet) Ambiguous inputs, many interacting factors, high-stakes deliverables Most capable tier (such as Opus), higher effort

docs.t: Choosing a Model and Effort Level
docs.x: A clear checklist applied to 800 standard agreements, with a lawyer reviewing every flag, is structured work: a fast tier is defensible because the human gate, not the tier, protects the outcome. "It's legal work" or "it's about people" does not by itself require the top tier; the complexity and stakes of the specific step do.

docs.t: Choosing a Model and Effort Level
docs.x: A defensible choice ties each task to evidence: 1. Test the candidate tier on a few real examples against the quality standard. 2. Keep the lower setting if it meets the bar; move up only if it does not. 3. Explain the trade-off: quality needed, speed, and usage or cost. Ticket tagging runs on the fast tier: high volume, low stakes, easy to fix. Quarterly strategy memos run on the most capable tier with higher effort: complex and consequential. Using one setting for both would overspend on tagging or underdeliver on strategy.

Context and Memory Management. Context is a budget. Restart from a summary when a long chat drifts, persist stable decisions to a Project, rely on memory only for recurring facts, keep memory accurate by reviewing and deleting entries, and use incognito chats for conversations that should stay out of history and memory.

Every conversation has a working-memory limit. As a long chat approaches it, earlier messages are summarized to make room, and detailed instructions given early can lose force. Managing context is choosing deliberately among four moves.

docs.h: Restart, summarize, persist or rely on memory
docs.x: Move When How Restart A long chat has drifted, or a genuinely new task begins New chat; Project instructions and knowledge carry over, the old thread does not Summarize The thread holds decisions worth keeping Ask for decisions, work in progress and open questions; start the new chat with that summary Persist Information every future chat needs Rules in Project instructions, facts and decisions in Project knowledge Memory Recurring facts about you and your work Let memory carry role, preferences, recurring context Chats in the same Project share its instructions and knowledge, but not each other's threads . A teacher's rule "no student devices" held all morning and slipped after two hours. The fix is a fresh chat with the rules summarized, or the rule in Project instructions, not repeating it in the same long chat.

Memory is useful only if it is current. Treat it like a working file: - Review stored memories regularly. - Edit or delete entries that no longer hold (a contact who left, last year's budget). - Scope memory: separate Projects keep project-scoped memory apart, so one client's context does not appear in another's work. - Reset after backing up what matters when stale entries are too many to fix one by one.

Incognito chats are kept out of chat history and memory and do not use existing memory. They suit exploratory or sensitive conversations outside Projects. They are still retained for a period under the default or the organization's retention settings and can appear in organizational exports. Incognito decides what is remembered, not whether data may be shared. Memory is best effort and per user. Firm rules belong in Project instructions, documents in knowledge, procedures in Skills.

A deliverable such as a business case, a vendor recommendation or a staffing plan has a lifecycle. Claude can help at every stage, but each stage needs the right method and a check before the next one builds on it.

Analysis Compute from internal data Code execution on uploaded files Spot-check figures and logic 4. Synthesis Draft the plan or recommendation Built only from checked inputs, each claim traceable The owner judges feasibility and decides A staffing plan built on a guessed utilization rate is a guess. Delegation and Workflow Redesign. Map a workflow step by step and assign each step as AI-executed, human-reviewed or human-retained, using reversibility, stakes, the need for human judgment or empathy, and accountability. Watch for over-delegation, halo delegation and review gates that quietly collapse.
The AI Fluency framework calls the choice of what to give AI Delegation . Workflow value comes from choosing which steps Claude does, not from handing it everything.

Criterion Question Reversibility If the output is wrong, can it be caught and undone before harm? Stakes What does an error cost, and who bears it? Human judgment or empathy Does the step need relationship, care or contextual judgment? Accountability Who answers for the outcome, and can they exercise that over an AI result?

Assignment Fits Example AI-executed Reversible, low-stakes, mechanical, easy to check Pulling order details into a summary; checking applications for missing documents Human-reviewed Claude adds value, but a person checks before use Drafting customer replies; summarizing messages that may contain urgent signals Human-retained Consequential, irreversible or accountable decisions; empathy-heavy work Approving payments; deciding admissions, claims or grades; handling appeals Assembling order history: AI-executed. Drafting the reply: human-reviewed. Approving a large refund or denying one after a dispute: human-retained. Setting next quarter's refund policy: human-retained.

docs.c: Low dollar value means low stakes
docs.x: - Over-delegation : giving AI a step whose risk calls for human ownership, such as unreviewed rejections of applicants. - Halo delegation : delegating a riskier step because an earlier one went well (password resets work, so let Claude approve finance access). - Collapsed gate : "AI drafts, human reviews" becomes "AI drafts" when reviewers approve without reading. A review nobody really does is no review. - Mapping the tools, not the work : assigning steps to whichever Skill exists instead of mapping the workflow first. A denied $800 claim can matter a great deal to the person, and still carries regulatory duties. Weigh stakes for the affected person, not only the amount. Delegating well also means not under-delegating: keeping mechanical extraction by hand wastes people's time.

Repeatable Workflow Design. Turn a recurring, manual or unstructured task into a workflow anyone can run the same way. Put shared context in a Project, procedures in Skills, live data behind connectors, and numbers in code-executed steps. Prove the gain, measure it, and hand it off with an owner and documentation.

"I use Claude" is a personal habit. "Our workflow uses Claude" is a process that gives the same quality whoever runs it. The signal that a task is ready: it recurs , its context is stable , and its output format is consistent .

Watch one full cycle and note every manual step you also did last time: Signal Fix Repetition : the same background pasted every run Project knowledge or instructions Correction : the same flaw fixed in every output A configuration change, often an instruction or a Skill Variance : different people get different results A shared Project and shared Skills Manual data copying A connector to the live source Hand or prose arithmetic A code-executed step A rule that always applies goes in instructions . Reference material every run needs goes in knowledge . A multi-step procedure goes in a Skill . Putting a fix in the wrong home is why some optimizations do not stick.

Run the new setup alongside the old approach for a few cycles before relying on it: a defect baked into a shared workflow spreads to everyone. Measure what mattered, such as time per cycle, revision rounds and consistency across people.

A workflow outlives its builder only if: - It lives where the owner can reach and edit it: a shared Project and shared Skills, not a personal account or chat history. - It is documented : purpose, inputs, steps, what is checked and by whom, and who to escalate to. - The logic is explained, especially what each Skill does and why. - The new owner has run it once under supervision. - Shared configuration has one owner who approves changes , so one person's preferences do not change everyone's output. A Project tuned for one teacher's class, or one analyst's habits, often carries assumptions that do not fit colleagues. Generalize it before sharing.

Choose shared configuration, the right home for each fix, connectors and code execution for data steps, a side-by-side trial, and documentation with an owner. Distractors ask people to write better personal prompts, rely on memory, keep the workflow in one person's account, or count Skills as a measure of success.

Capability Communication. Describe a Claude workflow to people with little AI familiarity accurately. Say what Claude does, what it cannot reliably do, which human checks remain and what outcomes are realistic, without overstating or understating, and calibrated to the audience.

Integrating Claude into a team means explaining it to people who did not build it: managers, clients, a risk committee, frontline staff. Credibility comes from accurate claims. Overstating loses trust at the first visible error; understating stops useful, safe work.

docs.h: A bounded description has three parts
docs.x: 1. What Claude does in this use case, specifically. 2. The human oversight that remains: who checks what, and when. 3. Realistic outcomes , with the evidence behind them. "Our AI reviews contracts automatically." versus "Claude drafts the first-pass summary and flags clauses that differ from our standard terms; our lawyer reviews and approves every change before signing. Review time dropped by about half in a three-week pilot."

- "Fully automated" or "handles X," which removes the human from the sentence. - "As good as our best people at everything." - "Error-free," "100% accurate," or "no review needed." - Predicting exact future numbers. Claude can model scenarios and ranges from stated assumptions; it cannot forecast exact revenue. Understating is also inaccurate: "It can't be trusted with anything important" ignores a proven, reviewed use that saves time.

Audience Wants Executives and boards Outcome, oversight in place, risk posture Technical or skeptical experts Failure modes, error rates found, the checks used Risk and compliance Controls: which outputs are reviewed, by whom, how errors are caught Affected staff What changes in their work and what they still own Customers What the assistant does and when a person takes over

A pilot result is real but bounded: "50% faster on one team over three weeks, with quality checked on 30 outputs" lets decision makers judge how far to extend it. Dropping the scope overstates certainty. "Anthropic is responsible for any errors" or "the AI decides" misstates who is accountable. The organization owns its outputs.

Pick the bounded version that names Claude's role, the human check and evidence-based outcomes, pitched to that audience. Project Configuration. Configure a Project by putting each requirement in the right slot. Behavior rules go in instructions, reference facts in knowledge, multi-step procedures in Skills, and accumulated context in project-scoped memory, with unrelated or competing work kept in separate Projects.

Using Claude means writing a good prompt today. Operating Claude means configuring an environment so every conversation starts from the right baseline. A Project is that environment for one recurring use case.

Slot Holds Example Instructions Behavior for every chat: tone, format defaults, verification habits, escalation rules "Cite the source document for every factual claim; flag what the documents do not cover" Knowledge Reference facts and documents The current rate card, policy manual, brand guide Skills Repeatable multi-step procedures and templates; set up at account level and usable in any Project Formatting proposals in the house template Project-scoped memory What the Project has settled over time Recurring concerns a business unit raised in earlier chats Ask what kind of thing each requirement is. A rule goes in instructions; a reference goes in knowledge; a procedure goes in a Skill. A behavior rule plus the facts it acts on usually needs two slots wired together: the citation rule in instructions, the documents it cites in knowledge.

- A 30-page manual pasted into instructions (bloats every chat; belongs in knowledge). - A 12-step procedure written as one instruction paragraph (steps get skipped; belongs in a Skill). - Firm rules left to memory (best effort and per user). - Every past version of a policy in knowledge (invites citing a superseded rule).

Unrelated or competing work streams belong in separate Projects . Project-scoped memory keeps one client's context out of another client's chats. Instructions such as "keep the clients apart" are not isolation. On Team and Enterprise plans, share a Project only with the people who need it, especially for sensitive work such as performance reviews. A procedure used by every client Project should be one Skill reused everywhere, not hand-edited copies that drift apart.

Items list requirements for a recurring use case and ask where each belongs, or how to fix a muddled Project. Sort each requirement into rule, reference, procedure or continuity, and isolate unrelated work. Connector and Knowledge Management. Give a workflow the sources it needs and no more. Connect live sources that change often, upload stable or point-in-time material, curate uploads to one current version, and keep connected knowledge scoped, current and free of noise.
What Claude knows in a workflow comes from two places: files you upload and sources you connect . Choosing well, and keeping both clean, decides whether answers stay current and relevant.

Upload Connector What it is A point-in-time copy Live access to a source you can already reach Best for Stable material (a brand guide), or analysis that must be tied to one frozen version Material that changes (a weekly catalog, today's email, the calendar) Risk Goes stale silently when the source changes Too broad a connection adds noise and exposure A product catalog updated weekly in Drive: connect it. A brand guide updated once a year: upload it to the Project and replace it when it changes.

- Connectors work within your own permissions . Claude cannot reach a shared mailbox you cannot open. - Each connector has defined actions. Some can draft or send only with your approval, and admins can restrict actions, for example search allowed and sending blocked. - On Team and Enterprise plans, admins decide which connectors are enabled and for whom. - A connector may return only part of a file; a Drive read may extract the text without processing embedded images. Learn a connector's boundary before building a workflow on it, so a limit is not mistaken for a bug.

- One current version of each document; remove superseded versions when you add new ones. - De-duplicate : two copies of the same interview make its themes look twice as common. - Label inputs so their role is clear ("approved policy," "draft responses"). - Prune what is unrelated to the Project's purpose; noise in is noise out. - Scope connections to the folders the workflow needs, such as executed contracts, not all drafts. Connecting the whole company drive brings in drafts, duplicates and data the task should not touch. Least privilege applies to knowledge too.

Match the source to how often it changes, scope connections, curate to one current version, and recognize permission and capability boundaries. Persistent-Instruction Design. Write persistent instructions precise enough that two people would read them the same way. Put what applies every time in the instructions and what changes in each request, and anticipate the edge cases and limits that would otherwise make outputs vary.

Persistent instructions, such as a Project's instructions, apply to every conversation without anyone remembering to add them. That makes them powerful, and it makes vague ones costly: they fail silently, in every chat.

docs.c: Would two people read it the same way?
docs.x: "Be concise" returns two lines for one person and two pages for another. "At most 150 words unless asked for more" is read the same by everyone. Vague Precise "Write good summaries." "List each decision as a bullet; list each action as owner, task, due date; mark unassigned actions 'owner TBD'." "Follow our standards." Name them: format, length, citation rule, audience, plus one example of a good output. "Help patients with their questions." "Scheduling questions only. Refer any medical question to the care team."

Persistent instructions Per-request prompt Tone, sign-off, format defaults Today's document or data Guardrails ("never promise refunds"; "flag what the documents do not cover") The specific customer, case or question How known edge cases are handled One-off variations ("this time, casual") When an add-on applies (when to include a security appendix) Temporary facts (today's delay at one warehouse) Anything typed at the start of every chat is a candidate for persistent instructions. Anything that changes each time belongs in the request.

Outputs vary most on cases the instructions did not foresee. Name the known edge cases and how to handle them, set a fallback for what the source does not cover ("refer to finance"), and say how to adapt for each known audience. A multi-step procedure that the instructions trigger belongs in a Skill.

When one task needs a different tone, do not delete the default. Name the exception in the instructions or state it in that request.

Configuration Lifecycle and Degradation. When a configuration that used to work starts producing worse output, trace the symptom to its layer (instructions, knowledge freshness, Skill version or accumulated memory), fix that layer, confirm recovery, and prevent recurrence with a regular review.

Configurations age. A standing instruction written for last year's process, a knowledge base holding superseded documents, a Skill that is out of date, or memory full of old facts will degrade output quietly, with no error message. The skill is to find the responsible layer, not to start rewriting prompts.

Symptom Likely layer Fix Cites an old price, policy or template Knowledge : a stale or duplicate document Replace it; remove old versions Uses another client's terms, a departed person, an old preference Memory : accumulated, cross-workstream or outdated entries Edit or delete entries; keep work streams in separate Projects The same format error in every run; changed right after a Skill update Skill version Check, correct and re-upload the Skill, or ask its owner Follows an old scope or a dated detail exactly Instructions : no longer match the current process Update the instruction; keep changing facts in knowledge Output that changed right after an upload points to knowledge; right after a Skill update, to the Skill. If instructions and Skills are unchanged, they cannot explain a change in output.

Use-Case Appropriateness. Classify each proposed use of Claude as appropriate, appropriate with safeguards, or inappropriate, with a documented rationale. Use the delegation criteria and the Anthropic Usage Policy, define any safeguard as who reviews what and when, and check third-party Skills and connectors before enabling them.
Governance is a practitioner skill: the policy sets the boundary, and you decide, use case by use case, whether a proposal is appropriate. "It feels risky" is not a decision anyone can review.

Classification Typical profile Example Appropriate Reversible, low consequence, grounded, normal review Drafting internal FAQ answers from approved policies Appropriate with safeguards Useful, but stakes or accountability need a defined human gate Drafting replies to complaints, checked by an agent before sending Inappropriate Consequence, irreversibility, need for human judgment, or the Usage Policy rules it out Final unreviewed clinical, legal, eligibility or discipline decisions; fake reviews Screen with the delegation criteria (reversibility, consequence, need for human judgment or empathy, accountability) and the Anthropic Usage Policy , which sets out prohibited uses and extra requirements for some higher-risk uses, such as review by a qualified professional and telling consumers they are dealing with AI. Organizational policy can add stricter rules.

docs.c: A safeguard is a defined gate
docs.x: The criteria interact. A condolence message is low-stakes and reversible, yet a person should own it because empathy matters. A financial summary is consequential, yet appropriate when a named reviewer signs off before it is used. Name the criterion that decides the call and the human role that must own the work. State who reviews (the accountable role), what they check (the specific risk: accuracy, fairness, policy) and when (before the output is used). "We'll keep a human in the loop" is not a gate.

A Skill runs with whatever access the session already has; a connector reaches data and may act on it. Before enabling either, check: - Source : Anthropic-provided or organization-approved is the lower-risk start; an unknown publisher needs review. Internal does not mean vetted. - Reach : what it could read or do, and whether that is proportional to the task (least privilege). - Appropriateness : whether it is the right tool at all. Outcomes: enable , escalate to the admin or security team, or decline . A new version that reaches further needs a fresh check. A disclaimer, a notice or advance consent does not supply the judgment and accountability a consequential decision needs.

Items describe a proposed use, a Skill or a connector and ask for the classification, the missing safeguard, or the right action. Weigh the criteria, check the Usage Policy, define gates in who-what-when form, and match access to purpose. Distractors approve because a better model is used, add disclaimers, trust internal origin or popularity, or trial risky access live.

Data Protection in Practice. Know the data's sensitivity before it enters any feature. Classify it, share only what the task needs, de-identify thoroughly (including free text and rare details), use only approved paths for regulated data, and use memory and incognito controls for what they actually do.
Most data leaks are routine decisions made without thinking: a spreadsheet uploaded as is, a personal account used because it was faster. Data protection is the habit of deciding before the upload.

Tier Examples Handling Green: safe to use Published material, anonymized aggregates, internal documents cleared for wide sharing Normal use Yellow: review first Internal-only documents, names and contact details, unannounced deals Check policy; minimize; approved workspace Red: keep out unless an approved path exists Health, financial and government-regulated data, credentials, third-party confidential material Confirm an approved, compliant path first; otherwise keep it out and escalate When unsure between two tiers, treat the data as the more sensitive one until confirmed.

docs.h: Share only what the task needs
docs.x: Trends by region need no customer names; a summary for leadership needs no witness identities. Remove what the task does not depend on before upload. Asking Claude to ignore or anonymize data after upload still shares it.

- Direct identifiers : names, IDs, account numbers, emails. - Quasi-identifiers : a unique job title plus a hire date, a rare condition, a small department's numbers. - Free text : comments, notes and tickets that say "This is Maria from Lakeside Dental." Finding duplicate customer records needs the names and addresses. When the task depends on the identifiers, redaction is not the answer: use an approved path for that data, or keep it out.

Control Does Does not Incognito chat Keeps the chat out of history and memory Make restricted data safe to share; it is still retained under retention policy Memory controls Stop details persisting across chats; review and delete entries Change what was already shared Code execution Processes uploaded files in a sandbox Decide whether the file should have been uploaded Approved workspace Provides the organization's agreed terms and controls, such as agreements needed for health data Remove the need to minimize data For regulated data, settle "is this workspace approved for this data?" before "how do I handle it here?"

Items show a dataset, a policy and a proposed action. Pick the step that classifies first, minimizes and de-identifies before upload, uses the approved path, and sets memory to match sensitivity. Distractors rely on incognito, restricted sharing of identifiable data, anonymizing after upload, removing names only, or personal accounts.

Policy, Ethics, and Diligence. Compare how people actually use Claude with what the AI policy requires. Diagnose each gap as a compliance breach, a policy gap or a training gap, recognize ethical risks such as bias and transparency failures, and choose the corrective action that closes the gap at its cause.

A policy that is followed only when someone is watching is not governance. Diligence in the AI Fluency framework is taking responsibility for AI-assisted work: using it ethically, being transparent about AI involvement, and verifying what you ship.

Gap What you see Corrective action Policy gap The policy is silent on a real practice (media replies, translation, how outputs are shared) Propose a policy update; put an interim control in place now Training gap A clear rule exists, but people do not know or understand it (new hires never shown it, an update never rolled out) Training and communication, and a check that it reached people Compliance breach A clear, known rule was not followed (review skipped, restricted data in a personal account) Contain the exposure, correct it, reinforce the rule; address what pushed people off the compliant path Layoff notices sent without the required HR review: breach. Customer letters translated with Claude, which the policy never mentions: policy gap. An analyst who never learned the memory rule for client work: training gap, after containing the exposure.

docs.h: Make the compliant path the default
docs.x: Diligence lapses often come from pressure or friction: reviews skipped on Friday afternoons, a slow approved workspace. A built-in gate, a confirmation step or adjusted deadlines change the pattern; a one-off reminder or blame does not.

- Bias : patterns across outputs, such as women described by personality and men by achievement, smaller discounts in certain ZIP codes, or non-standard English summarized as "unclear." Look across the set, not one output; investigate even without explicit intent. - Transparency failures : required AI disclosure omitted, paraphrased text presented as direct quotes, invented testimonials. - Diligence lapses : sign-off without checking because "Claude is always right."

Reason it through: who is affected, what could go wrong, what a fair outcome requires, what disclosure the setting calls for. Document the reasoning and safeguards. When the stakes are large or the question is beyond your standing, escalate to the AI governance or ethics function with that reasoning, rather than reinterpreting the policy in your own favor. "Claude wrote it" is never a defense. The person who ships the work owns it.

Items describe observed usage and ask what kind of gap it is, which ethical risk it shows, or which corrective action fits. Diagnose first (silent policy, unknown rule, ignored rule), then fix at the cause. Distractors treat a policy gap as a training failure, discipline people for breaking unwritten rules, ban tools wholesale, or wait for complaints.
